job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Elena Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a senior field researcher at the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My mornings start with coffee in the kitchen of the flat I share with my mother and my grandmother, in Lisbon. I finished a computer science degree in July with a plain pass. My final project predicted bus delays from timetable data, and my supervisor said it was neat but under-tested. Then I open my laptop and, honestly, I talk to an AI model for an hour. It helps me tidy my CV, explains new frameworks and plans the day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Where do you feel strongest in all this, and where weakest?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: After that I send applications, usually five or six, and work on a side project: a little app that helps my grandmother remember her pills. I've had no internships, because I spent summers helping at my aunt's café.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's take AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, the tools are useful but I never believed they'd change everything overnight. I'd tell my friends we should be happy to have helpers and stop panicking. Online I'd post a short thread about the tools I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it means my plan stays the same. I build things, apply, and hope someone sees past the plain pass. My family has savings, so I'm not scared about food or rent. Some of my friends are shaken by no replies, but I don't take it personally yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make the pill app into a proper portfolio piece and put it on the public repository with a write-up. I'd apply to 30 jobs a month and ask two lecturers for introductions. I'd also try to get one small paid gig on a freelance board, even 100 euros, so my CV shows a customer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little itchy to start earning, so I don't feel stuck in my family's flat forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned friends shaken by no replies. What do you tell them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the replies are about fit, not worth. I tell my friends to send fewer, better applications and to show something working. A small demo says more than a grade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you use AI for your CV and your planning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's fast, and I check what it says. It catches things I'd never notice, like a vague line that says nothing. I wouldn't send anything without reading it twice.

I'd post a short thread about the tools I like.
think: My plan stays the same: build things and hope someone sees past the **plain pass**.
Family savings mean I'm not scared about **food or rent**.
do: Turn the pill app into a **portfolio piece** with a public write-up.
Send **30 applications a month** and win one small paid freelance gig.
feel: **Calm**, a little itchy to start earning and leave my family's flat.

fieldNote: Uses AI **daily** and checks what it writes before sending it.

The pill app for her grandmother is a **real** product with a real user.

steps.text: Finish the pill reminder app and publish it with a write-up
Send 30 applications a month to Lisbon software firms
Use an AI model to review every CV and cover letter draft

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's take Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the real thing and public support has to catch up. Governments should pay for retraining and make firms show when software replaces staff. Among friends I'd say don't wait for permission, learn the tools properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's mixed. The tasks AI takes first are coding, checking and writing, which are the entry-level parts of a junior developer's day. So fewer junior roles, and the ones left want people who can direct the tools. I'd say I'm better placed than my classmates because I already work with them every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd retarget at roles where I direct the AI: junior automation analyst, QA with AI tools, or a support engineer. I'd take a short course on building agents and publish three small examples. I'd also go to a meetup every fortnight, because jobs come through people. And I'd keep a month of savings in cash, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a mix of excitement and nerves. I'm moving fast, but I know the speed also helps firms replace people like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said speed helps firms replace people like you. How do you feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not great. I'm learning the thing that might take my entry role. But refusing wouldn't help, so I'd rather be the one pointing the tool than the one it points at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about most at the meetup?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people who don't have a family flat to fall back on. They don't get the six months I get to experiment. I'd want public money for them, not just advice from people like me.

say: I'd say governments must **pay for retraining** and make firms show when software replaces staff.
I'd tell friends to learn the tools properly.
think: Junior roles shrink, and the rest want people who can **direct** the tools.
I'm better placed than classmates because I use AI **daily**.
do: Target **automation analyst** and QA roles, and publish three small agent examples.
Go to a **meetup** every fortnight and keep a month's savings in cash.
feel: **Uneasy**: excited and nervous, aware speed also helps firms replace people like me.
S1.quote: I'd rather be the one pointing the tool than the one it points at.
fieldNote: Moves **first**, in line with her adaptive profile.
Aware of **privilege**: her family flat gives her room others lack.
Asks for **public money** for people with no cushion.

steps.text: Apply for junior automation analyst and AI-assisted QA roles
Take a short course on building agents and publish three examples
Use AI daily to draft test plans and review my own code
Sign petitions for public retraining funds

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's take AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have almost no time, and politicians must act now. Two years is not enough to rewrite schools, pensions or benefits. I'd say it online, and not just as a post: I'd email my representative.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be scared in a hard-to-explain way. I'm one of the people who knows the tools, and I still don't think there's a place for a junior who adds little beyond them. Almost any thinking job is under threat in 2028, and robots for hands-on work come around 2031. So even a trade only buys time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any paid job in the first month, even outside tech, so there's income and a reference. I'd apply for a master's in something that blends fields, like AI policy or safety, since people will be needed to check the systems. I'd move savings into a safe account and stop buying anything extra. And I'd spend time with my grandmother, because she keeps saying life is about people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, deep down. Having a plan helps, but the plan could be useless in two years, and that's hard to feel good about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a trade only buys time. What does that do to your thinking about the master's?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes me think a degree might not protect anyone either. But I'd do the master's for the network rather than the certificate, because it keeps me near people who are working out what comes next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your mother say that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd make soup, and she'd tell me we have each other. She'd also say we can't carry the whole family on her wage if I don't earn. We'd talk about it properly for the first time.

say: I'd say two years is **not enough** for schools, pensions or benefits.
I'd email my representative, not just post online.
think: Even a junior who knows the tools might have **no place** by 2028.
Hands-on trades only **buy time**, since robots arrive around 2031.
do: Take **any paid job** in the first month, even outside tech.
Apply for a master's in **AI policy or safety** and move savings to a safe account.
feel: **Anxious**: my plan could be useless in two years.
S2.quote: I'd do the master's for the network rather than the certificate, because it keeps me near people who are working out what comes next.
fieldNote: Her fluency with AI gives her **no comfort** about the junior role.
Moves toward **policy** and safety work, the part she thinks humans must check.
Talks about **family** more here than in any other scenario.

steps.text: Take any paid job within the first month, even outside tech
Apply for a master's in AI policy or safety
Move savings into a safe account and stop extra spending
Email my representative asking for a transition plan for graduates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's take AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a window and we must use it. I'd want a public plan for retraining and a ban on firms using AI to dodge their duties. Online I'd write long posts that three people read.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel pretty positive about my position. I'd have five years to get an entry job, become a person firms can't easily swap, and maybe be a technical lead by 2031. Robots for the hands-on side come around 2034, so even a physical career would hold a bit longer. The risk is everyone else is also learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a job inside a year, preferably in a firm that builds for hospitals or public services, where people can't be fully removed. I'd keep studying part-time, probably a postgraduate certificate in data ethics. And I'd save at least a third of every pay cheque, because I want a flexible fund if the market turns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a lively way. I'd feel I have a map, even if it might change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the risk is everyone else also learning. Who is 'everyone'?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every graduate with a laptop. The tools make competition global. A firm in Warsaw or Manila can do what I do for less. I'd have to be good at being close to people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean by being close to people?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being in the room with the users, not just writing code in the background. My grandma is a user, and I know when the pill app confuses her. That's what a remote team can't copy easily.

say: I'd say five years is a **window** and we must use it.
I'd want a **public retraining plan** and rules stopping firms dodging their duties.
think: I'd feel **positive** about my position with five years to build a record.
The risk is every graduate with a laptop is also **learning**.
do: Land a job in a firm building for **hospitals or public services**.
Study a part-time certificate in **data ethics** and save a third of each pay.
feel: **Uneasy** in a lively way: I'd feel I have a map that might change.
S3.quote: My grandma is a user, and I know when the pill app confuses her.
fieldNote: Names **closeness to users** as her edge over remote competitors, a point she returns to twice.
Realistic about **global** competition for junior work, since firms abroad can do her work for less.

steps.text: Land a job at a firm building software for hospitals or councils
Study a part-time postgraduate certificate in data ethics
Save a third of every pay cheque in a flexible fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's take AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to build something good, if we choose to. I'd tell friends to learn things that last, like how to work with people and how to check a machine. Online I'd probably share plans for a small project.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's the calmest of the three. A decade gives me time to work, fail, switch fields and still be young by 2036. Robots for hands-on work would only be around 2039, so there's even more time for any kind of job. I'd also hope we use the time to rewrite the rules around benefits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start in a junior role and rotate through three kinds of work in five years: data, product and support. I'd keep building small public tools, like the pill app, and maybe turn it into a tiny business with my aunt's help. I'd save steadily, and vote for parties that fund retraining and care work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like a hard but fair world, where I can move first and still have time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the tiny business look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An app for older people and their families, with a small subscription from the family. My aunt knows lots of neighbours who would try it. It wouldn't make me rich, but it'd be mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the thing you'd regret not doing in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd regret spending the whole time looking at screens and missing my grandma's last years. I'd want to build things and also be at the table. I think about that more than the jobs.

say: I'd tell friends to learn things that last: **working with people** and checking a machine.
I'd share plans for a small project online.
think: A decade gives me time to **work, fail, switch fields** and still be young in 2036.
I'd hope we use the time to rewrite the rules on **benefits**.

feel: **Calm**: a hard but fair world where I can still move first.

fieldNote: The long horizon lets her talk about **values**, not just jobs.
Business idea comes straight from her **grandmother** and her aunt's network.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most. It leaves no room to try, and I'm the sort of person who learns by trying. What would help is public money for retraining that arrives quickly, and firms being made to hire and train some juniors.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say people think my generation is glued to AI and doesn't care. We care a lot, we're just also practical. I use these tools because I want a seat at the table when decisions are made.

headlineQuote: We care a lot, we're just also practical. I use these tools because I want a seat at the table when decisions are made.
portrait: Elena is **23**, a computer science graduate with a plain pass, living with her mother and grandmother in Lisbon.
She uses AI **every day**, checks its work, and sees herself as someone who learns by doing.
She is progressive and wants **public retraining** and rules for firms, but would act herself first.
Her family cushion makes her **calm** in mild worlds and anxious only in the 2028 one.
Her best idea, a **pill reminder app**, comes from her grandmother, and shows where she plans to build her career.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture worries her most because she learns by trying and would have no room to try.
whatWouldHelp: Fast **public money** for retraining, and a rule that firms must hire and train some juniors.
